title: How to Pay an Independent Contractor in 2026: Step by Step
summary: How to pay an independent contractor: W-9 or W-8BEN, payment methods, the new $2,000 1099-NEC threshold, and what changes when they work abroad.
body_markdown:
**To pay an independent contractor in the US, confirm they really are a contractor, collect a Form W-9 before the first payment, agree the terms in writing, pay each invoice through a traceable method like ACH, and file Form 1099-NEC by January 31 for anyone you paid $2,000 or more in 2026.** If the contractor lives and works outside the US, the form changes to a W-8BEN and the 1099 drops out.


That is the whole job in one paragraph. The rest of this guide walks through each step, the payment methods and what they cost you in time, and the mistakes that turn a simple payment into a tax problem. If your team is spread across Latin America, the section on paying contractors outside the US is the one to read.


## Key takeaways


- Classification comes first. If you control how, when and where the work gets done, the IRS may see an employee, not a contractor.
- Get the tax form before you pay: a W-9 for US persons, a W-8BEN for foreign individuals. No form, no payment.
- The 1099-NEC threshold rose from $600 to $2,000 per contractor for payments made in 2026. Payments made in 2025 still use $600.
- Payments you make by card or through a payment app are reported by the processor on Form 1099-K, so they stay off your 1099-NEC.
- A contractor who works 100% outside the US and gives you a valid W-8BEN gets no 1099-NEC and, in most cases, no US withholding.
- Paying a team abroad is where most of the friction lives: local invoicing rules, currency and payout speed. That is the problem[Ontop solves for companies paying contractors internationally](https://www.getontop.com/solutions/pay-international-contractors) .


## How do you pay an independent contractor, step by step?


Paying a contractor is a five-step routine you set up once and repeat every pay cycle.


1. **Confirm the classification.** Make sure the relationship is a real contractor relationship.
2. **Collect the tax form.** W-9 for US contractors, W-8BEN for foreign individuals.
3. **Sign an agreement.** Scope, rate, invoicing cadence and payment terms.
4. **Pay against invoices.** Pick a method that leaves a clean record.
5. **Report at year end.** Issue Form 1099-NEC to US contractors over the threshold.


## Step 1: Confirm the person is really a contractor


Before money moves, check the relationship. The IRS looks at three things: behavioral control (do you direct how the work is done?), financial control (who pays for tools, can the person profit or lose?) and the relationship itself (benefits, permanence, whether the work is core to your business).


A contractor sets their own hours, uses their own equipment, works for other clients and invoices you for results. If you are setting a schedule, assigning a manager and expecting them in every standup, you may be looking at an employee. Misclassification can mean back payroll taxes, penalties and benefit claims, so it is worth ten minutes now. Our[contractor vs employee test](https://www.getontop.com/calculator/contractor-vs-employee) gives you a quick read, and this guide covers[the real cost of misclassification](https://www.getontop.com/blog/contractor-misclassification-risks) .


## Step 2: Collect the right tax form before the first payment


The form you collect depends on who the contractor is, not where you are.


Contractor Form you collect Year-end reporting


US citizen or resident, or a US business Form W-9 (name, address, SSN or EIN) Form 1099-NEC if you paid $2,000 or more in 2026


Foreign individual working outside the US Form W-8BEN No 1099-NEC


Foreign company Form W-8BEN-E No 1099-NEC


Keep the form on file; you do not send it to the IRS. If a US contractor will not give you a taxpayer identification number, you are required to apply backup withholding of 24% to their payments, which is a good reason to make the W-9 part of onboarding rather than an afterthought.


## Step 3: Put the terms in writing


A short agreement prevents most payment disputes. It should cover the scope of work, the rate (hourly, fixed or milestone), how and when the contractor invoices you, your payment terms (for example, net 15), who owns the work product, and how either side can end the engagement. Here is a deeper look at[what goes into an independent contractor agreement](https://www.getontop.com/blog/independent-contractor-agreement) .


Ask for an invoice for every payment. It should show the contractor's legal name, the period or deliverable, the amount and currency, and their payment details. Invoices are what tie your payments to your 1099 totals, so keep them all. If your contractors need a template, point them to this[contractor invoice guide](https://www.getontop.com/blog/contractor-invoice) .


## Step 4: Choose how you will send the money


Any method works if it leaves a record you can match to an invoice. What changes is speed, cost and who reports the payment.


Method Speed Good for Who reports it


ACH / direct deposit 1 to 3 business days Recurring payments to US contractors You, on Form 1099-NEC


Check Days, plus mail time Occasional payments You, on Form 1099-NEC


Domestic wire Same or next business day Large or urgent payments You, on Form 1099-NEC


Credit card or payment app (PayPal, Venmo for business) Minutes to days Small, one-off payments The processor, on Form 1099-K


International wire Several business days, with bank and FX fees Occasional payments abroad No 1099 if the contractor is foreign and works abroad


Contractor payment platform Varies by provider Paying several contractors, especially abroad Depends on the contractor's form


One detail that saves cleanup in January: if you paid part of a contractor's fees by card or through a payment app, leave those amounts out of their 1099-NEC. The processor reports them.


## Step 5: File Form 1099-NEC at year end


Form 1099-NEC reports what you paid a US contractor during the calendar year. The rules that matter:


- **Threshold.** $2,000 or more paid to one contractor in calendar year 2026, up from $600. The change comes from the 2025 tax law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and applies to payments made after December 31, 2025. For 2025 payments, which you report in January 2026, the threshold is still $600.
- **Deadline.** January 31 for both copies: one to the contractor and one to the IRS.
- **How to file.** If you file 10 or more information returns in a year, counting all types together, you must file electronically, for example through the IRS's free Information Returns Intake System (IRIS).
- **What to include.** Payments for services by check, ACH or wire. Leave out card and payment app payments, and payments to most corporations.


Late or wrong forms carry penalties per form, and they grow the longer you wait. Check the current figures in the IRS instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC before you file, and confirm state filing rules too, since many states require their own copy.


## What changes when the contractor is outside the US?


A lot of US companies now pay contractors in Latin America, and the rules are simpler on the US side than most people expect. If the contractor is a foreign individual and does all the work outside the US, the income is foreign-source. Collect a W-8BEN, keep it on file, and you generally have no 1099-NEC, no Form 1042-S and no US withholding. The picture changes if the person does part of the work while physically in the US, so track that.


The work moves to the local side and to the payment itself:


- **Local invoicing.** Many countries require contractors to issue a local tax invoice for exported services, such as DIAN invoicing in Colombia, the CFDI in Mexico or the factura E in Argentina.
- **Currency.** Decide whether you pay in USD or local currency, and who absorbs conversion costs.
- **Payout speed and fees.** International wires stack bank fees and can take days, which adds up when you pay a whole team every month.
- **Classification still applies.** Local labor law decides whether the relationship is really contracting, not your contract template.

## Common mistakes when paying contractors


- **Paying before the W-9 or W-8BEN is on file.** Chasing a form in January is harder than collecting it on day one.
- **Treating a contractor like staff.** Fixed hours, a company laptop and a manager are classification red flags.
- **Adding card payments to the 1099-NEC.** They belong on the processor's 1099-K, and double reporting confuses the contractor's return.
- **Sending a 1099 to a foreign contractor.** If they work fully abroad and gave you a W-8BEN, it is the wrong form.
- **Paying without invoices.** Without them, your records cannot back up your year-end totals.

## Frequently asked questions


### Do I need to send a 1099 to every independent contractor?


No. You send Form 1099-NEC to US contractors you paid $2,000 or more during 2026 for services ($600 for 2025 payments), excluding payments made by card or payment app and payments to most corporations. Foreign contractors who work outside the US do not get one.


### What is the best way to pay a 1099 contractor?


For recurring payments to US contractors, ACH or direct deposit is usually the simplest: low cost, one to three business days, and an easy record to match against invoices. For contractors abroad, a contractor payment platform avoids stacked wire and conversion fees.


### When is Form 1099-NEC due?


January 31 of the year after the payments, both to the contractor and to the IRS.


### Do I withhold taxes from an independent contractor's payments?


Normally no. Contractors pay their own income and self-employment taxes. The exception is backup withholding at 24% when a US contractor does not give you a valid taxpayer identification number.


### How do I pay an independent contractor in another country?


Collect a W-8BEN, sign an agreement, receive an invoice that meets local rules, and pay through an international method. If the work is done entirely outside the US, there is generally no 1099 and no US withholding.
